Capital One. What's in your wallet? Terms of fly. Details at CapitalOne.com.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
A schoolteacher and a parent are being praised for their efforts to end an elementary school shooting
in Bend, Oregon. This week, three children and a teacher were killed when a
16-year-old special needs student opened fire before he was shot and killed by a parent.
Ben Lapine's school superintendent, Stephen Cook, says it's time now to help people grieve.
Silver rail families are showing our community how to wrap our arms around our children,
to comfort and love and remind them that the adults in their schools
and in their lives deeply care about them.
A fast-moving fire has burned several homes in Southern California.
This hot, windy weather has gripped the region.
It's one of several burning in the area and has led to evacuations.
Steve Futterman reports from Forge County.
This fire, the Norte Fire, continues to burn in the foothills above us here in San Juan Capistrano
and next door in San Clemente. There are residential areas in these foothills.
Some homes have been burned. Some will be total losses.
The skies above us, just full of smoke.
Fire crews doing their best to attack the flames both on the ground and from the air
using fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters dropping both water and fire retardant.
While the winds continue to blow the only bit of good news, the winds aren't as strong as they were earlier today.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in San Juan Capistrano.
Demonstrators in France are hoping for an alliance between student protesters
and the yellow vest movement that mobilized against high gas prices in the government eight years ago.
As NPR's Salander Beardsley reports, an economic crisis could bring the movements together in what's being billed as a day of anger.
The French Interior Minister says 90 protest marches and 500 separate actions are planned across the country.
Social media posts indicate that there could be an alliance between the students who are protesting dilapidated facilities,
overcrowded classrooms and a lack of teachers, and a reconstituted yellow vest movement of angry white working class voters.
Everyone is demanding more government spending and protections against rising energy prices.
But with France mired in debt and with record high borrowing costs, the government has little room to maneuver.
Meanwhile, stores in some cities are boarding up their windows ahead of tomorrow's protests.
Eleanor Beardsley in Pierre News, Paris.
There were more problems with some big tech stocks and they caused Wall Street to close lower on Friday.
The S&P 500 lost 1.1 percent while the NASDAQ was down 2.1 percent and the Dow dropped 0.3 percent.
Chip companies pulled back as worries deepened about how long the AI build out will last.
You're listening to NPR News.
Thousands of people are being driven from their homes this weekend as heavy rains continue to fall in parts of Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina.
The rains are being driven by the climate pattern known as El Nino.
In one Paraguayan village along the Paraña River, the mayor says waters have risen to the highest level seen in more than 40 years.
Researchers are learning more about how psychology influences the ability to bounce back from a sports injury.
And Paris Willstone reports that it's not just about being physically well enough to return to activity.
A sizable share of people, about one in three, who undergo ACL surgery don't return to their previous level of sport.
Fear of being re-injured is often a big reason.
Shelby Bias directs the psychology of sports injury lab at UNC Chapel Hill.
In a new study, she and other researchers followed about 60 people recovering from ACL surgery and ran a series of physical and psychological tests.
It wasn't necessarily those objective factors or quad strength and hop symmetry that were predictive or associated with psychological readiness.
In her work at UNC, Bias is finding that certain approaches like mindfulness and grounding techniques can be helpful for people who are cleared to play,
but still struggle with anxiety and fear after their injury.
Willstone, NPR News.
The NCAA has filed a federal lawsuit against Ohio Governor Mike DeWine.
DeWine signed an executive order that allows Ohio colleges to let athletes who graduated in 2022 play a fifth year.
The order comes despite an NCAA rule that excludes athletes who have played in four seasons.
The group says the lawsuit will prevent the state from disrupting fair competition among schools.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
Learn more at Schwab.com.
